content.passage:
I'm Fuad. I want to tell you about my sister and two friends of mine.

Fatma is my young sister. She is short and very slim. She is 1 metre 10 centimetres tall and weighs 27 kilos. She has got long black hair and brown eyes. She works very hard at school and she is very good at Arabic. She quite likes English too. She is very helpful. She likes working in the garden at the weekend.

Ali is one of my friends. He is quite short and a bit fat. He is 1 metre 55 and weighs 63 kilos. Some of my friends say he is rude, but that is not true. He has got a bad memory, so he forgets things people say to him. Ali is also a bit lazy. He likes motor bikes and he is good at fixing them. He wants to buy a motor-bike, but he does not have enough money.

Hassan is another friend. He is the opposite of Ali. He is tall and slim. He is 1 metre 78 and he weighs 60 kilos. He has got a good memory and he is very hard-working. He does not like cars or motor-bikes. He likes animals and birds, so he goes walking in the mountains at the weekend. He also likes photography, so he takes his camera with him. His favourite bird is the black stork.

activities.compensates: Replaces teacher-led reading aloud and comprehension questions (PB14).

content.passage:
Hassan shook his young brother. 'Get up, Khalid,' he said. 'It's quarter past seven.'
'Go away. 'It's too early to get up,' said Khalid.
'OK. I'll see you when I get back,' said Hassan. 'I'm going to look for a black stork.'
Khalid sat up. 'Can I come?' he shouted.
'Yes, you can. I'm going to make some sandwiches,' Hassan replied.

Half an hour later, the two boys left the house. Hassan was carrying his camera. His brother was carrying a plastic bag with food and water in it.
'What does a black stork look like?' asked Khalid.
'It's a big, beautiful bird,' said Hassan. 'It lives in Africa for half the year and it lives here for the other half.'
'Is it here now?' Khalid asked.
'I don't know,' Hassan replied. 'We'll see.'

'Hassan, it's half past ten,' said Khalid.
'I know,' replied Hassan. 'So what?'
'I'm tired and hot. I'm hungry and thirsty too,' replied Khalid.
'All right,' said Hassan, smiling. 'We'll stop here for a little bit.'
They sat down next to a rock. Hassan handed his brother a sandwich.
Khalid bit into it.
'It's beautiful here,' said Khalid.
'Yes, it is,' replied Hassan. 'The mountains are wonderful.' Suddenly, he put his hand on Khalid's arm.
'Look!' he whispered.
Khalid looked up.
'It's a falcon,' said Hassan quietly. 'Now, watch.'
The falcon suddenly fell out of the sky like a stone. A few seconds later, it was up and flying again. It was carrying something.
'It looks like a hare,' said Hassan. 'There are lots of hares in the mountains. That's its lunch.'
'Hare for lunch - that's better than a cheese and tomato sandwich,' said Khalid.

questions.question: The snake ___ the man's leg.
questions.explanation: The simple past tense of the irregular verb 'bite' is 'bit'.

options.feedback: Incorrect. 'Shake' is an irregular verb.
Excellent! 'Shook' is the past tense of 'shake'.
This is the past participle, used with 'has' or 'have'.

questions.question: He ___ his head when he didn't know the answer.
questions.explanation: The simple past tense of the irregular verb 'shake' is 'shook'.

options.feedback: Not quite. Remember the spelling rule for verbs ending in 'y'.
Correct! When a verb ends in a consonant + 'y', we change 'y' to 'ied'.
This is the present tense form.

questions.question: She ___ to my email yesterday.
questions.explanation: The past tense of 'reply' is 'replied'. The 'y' changes to 'i' before adding '-ed'.

activities.title: Talking About the Future
activities.instruction: Read the situation and Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the best way to talk about the future.
activities.compensates: This activity replaces the teacher-led open-pair practice for future forms mentioned in the Teacher Guide for PB15.

options.feedback: We use the present continuous for fixed arrangements, not for sudden decisions.
Correct! We use 'will' for spontaneous decisions made at the moment of speaking.
We use 'going to' for plans made before speaking, not for a sudden decision.

questions.question:
A: The phone is ringing! 
B: Don't worry, I ___ it.
questions.explanation: Use 'will' for offers and spontaneous decisions.

options.feedback: This is a fixed plan, so another form is better.
Perfect! We use the present continuous ('are going') for fixed arrangements in the future.
This is the present simple, used for schedules, not personal arrangements.

questions.question: I have bought the tickets. We ___ to the cinema on Friday.
questions.explanation: Use the present continuous for future arrangements that are already confirmed (like buying tickets).

options.feedback: This form is not used to talk about future plans.
'Will' is for predictions without evidence. 'Going to' is better for intentions.
Correct! We use 'going to' to talk about our plans and intentions for the future.

questions.question:
A: What are your plans after you finish school? 
B: I ___ a doctor.
questions.explanation: Use 'going to' to talk about future plans and intentions.
